I love this game.
Been playing this game for more than 4,500 hours (PvE, solo).
This review is aimed at the changes in the Enhanced version, not the game in general.
TL;DR: Superficially nice, but it offers nothing the legacy version doesn't have. 
(UI Slider?!? devs, hello?)

I stayed with the legacy version for a long time because I hesitated to set up my modlist every time they release a new engine update. Now I decided to make the switch a few days ago, but I am not excited about the Enhanced version at all.

The new graphics look really nice, but that's it. The shadows and lighting create an uncomfortable environment that is almost painful to play in for longer than a few minutes. It looks nice in the trailers, but actual gameplay is more than uncomfortable.

Worst of all is the UI. Everything in the HUD is way too small, except the Journey steps, which obscure half of the screen. On the other hand, everything in the Inventory and Knowledge tabs is HUGE. The icons are way too big, making the whole interface feel almost claustrophobic. It feels like a lazy mobile or console layout forced onto Pc players.

WHY is there no UI size slider?
I'll never understand how in the world game developers can basically create a new version of a game but completely ignore such a crucial element like the UI. Even worse, they didn't include any UI scaling whatsoever, leaving PC players completely stranded. 

EDIT: I almost forgot. Why does the camera zoom in and out like crazy when i have target lock activated? What in the world is this supposed to archieve? The only thing it causes is motion sickness. 
(Keep it as it was before. IT WAS FINE!!)

Fantastic exploration, visuals and sound design. Whoever they got working on sound effects needs a promotion and payrise, the sound in this game is amazing (I played with headphones). The game doesn't hold your hand and you have to read and interpret what the game expects you to do next, which is something I enjoy. You could call it a discount Elden Ring. There is a story but you have to go hunting for it and piece it all together. There is very little guidance. 

The bad is the combat is undercooked. All weapons feel the same except for having different armor penetration values, which makes the mace/hammer hands down best for everything because it has the highest armor pen. I tried switching to various other weapons but they purely underperformed. The hitboxes are bad and you have to basically hug enemies to be able to hit them which makes the spear with its range pointless. 

Whoever decided you couldn't repair legendary gear needs to be fired and replaced by the sound design guy, I reckon he can do a better job balancing gear and combat in this game. Yes I'm aware they added some smithy but I'm not slogging through some dungeon to repair gear. Its like they made things arbitrarily difficult to deter you from gearing yourself. Which leads to my next point.

Thralls/Companions are 4-5 times more effective at combat damage than you are because you end up gearing them with all the legendary equipment since there is no durability damage for their gear. So you end up feeling like a side character while your Thrall/Slave is this juggernaut tank with tiger tank plates for armor and hits like a howitzer. Just a poor feeling overall when I'm suppose to be the one pulling their chains.

Regardless of the negatives it was an enjoyable trek exploring the exiled lands. Lots to see and explore, interesting lore to uncover. If you are interested in exploration, story and Conan lore then I would grab it when on sale. Don't expect deep combat mechanics.

Conan Exiles – this is a game about a time so ancient that logic was yet to be born. It is a land of might and magic, legendary creatures, and desert-mountain-climbing crocodiles. A land where common sense has yet to be invented and master craftsmen make things purely by guesswork.

This positive review is based on a solo, heavily modded playthrough, so let’s start with the cons first.

I don’t know why, but "the game" (which is what I’ll be calling the devs from now on) really hates logic and common sense in general. It’s practically allergic to it. If you play vanilla, you are bound to suffer brain damage just from how stupid things can get in there.

However, its biggest problem is that the game has a split personality and suffers from constant inconsistency because of that. Quality comes side-by-side with a careless, slapped-together mess. There is a blatant inconsistency in styles; the game isn't sure if it wants to be realistic or cartoonishly exaggerated. Those styles don't mix and realism works much better here, I hope they focus on that.

Every update traditionally breaks something — and no, I am not talking about the mods. Usually it’s unintentional, but that isn’t always the case. They nearly ruined the fighting system; daggers are barely playable now, and they did that one on purpose! No one asked for it. It was a freaking whim that scarred the game forever.

You will see brilliant talent and creativity right next to obnoxious laziness. Those silly attempts to sell you reskinned crap right alongside something new and beautiful make this game a living absurdity...

But then, there are mods, and this is where the game starts shining. Yes, this is another beautiful example of a game saved by its players, just like Skyrim. It's a testament to what happens when players see the raw potential of a game and pour their brilliance into exploring it. Without mods, this game would be long dead, just like Skyrim.

But it isn’t dead, and here is why.

The recent update to Unreal Engine 5 was a success; we’ve got the same old jank, but now it looks fantastic. They are finally fixing collisions and the navmesh, the poor quality of which has plagued this game for years. There’s still plenty to be done, but I can see the progress. 
Of course, the update didn’t go completely smoothly — it wouldn’t be Funcom without a screw-up — but it actually went smoother than most of us expected, and it seems to be moving in the right direction. It feels like the side of the studio that actually possesses vision and ambition has taken the wheel, which brings hope.

And now, for the real explanation behind my thumbs-up.

The game (mods included, obviously) allows you to build your own world, and I am having a blast doing that. I create quests. I create NPCs. I’m building entire cities, and then I attack them... I turned the game into an absurdity of my own design, and there is absolutely nothing that can replace that feeling. You are only limited by your imagination, and I have yet to see the limits of mine. It can be the ultimate chill zone, a brutal challenge zone, or both. It’s entirely up to you.

Recommended. This is still the best all-around survival crafting game in its class.

I've played a lot of survival crafting games, and despite its numerous flaws, questionable business practices, occasionally hilarious combat, and my increasingly concerning collection of scantily clad female thralls, *Conan Exiles* remains the best all-around experience in the genre.

First, the art direction is absolutely fantastic. The Exiled Lands feel like a genuinely dangerous, ancient, and often hostile world. From the scorching deserts and forgotten ruins to the frozen northern wastes and the oppressive jungles, there's a tremendous sense of atmosphere. The world feels like it existed long before you arrived and will continue existing long after something horrible eats you. There's a wonderful sense of mystery to the environments, and the developers clearly understood the assignment when it came to capturing Robert E. Howard's brutal, decadent sword-and-sorcery setting.

And unlike a lot of survival games, Conan actually feels dangerous, particularly early on. You're not some chosen hero destined to save the world. You're a half-naked idiot with a rock, and practically everything wants to murder you. Even after you've established yourself, wandering into the wrong area unprepared can result in a quick and thoroughly humiliating death. That sense of lethality is something many other survival games lose far too quickly.

The combat, meanwhile, is an interesting mixture of genuinely enjoyable mechanics and absolute slapstick nonsense. Sometimes you're engaged in a satisfying, bloody duel with a dangerous enemy. Other times you're watching your thrall attempt to navigate a doorway while an enemy performs what appears to be an interpretive dance before launching itself into low orbit. Hit detection can be questionable, animations occasionally have a mind of their own, and the AI sometimes seems to have suffered a traumatic brain injury. But there's something almost endearing about the jank. At least until it gets you killed.

The building system is another major strength. The sheer variety of architectural pieces, decorations, furniture, and themed construction sets is outstanding. You can build anything from a miserable little desert shack to a sprawling fortress, an opulent palace, or a barbarian pleasure resort that would make Caligula blush. While *Enshrouded* arguably has the superior building mechanics, Conan's aesthetic variety and ability to create genuinely lived-in settlements are exceptional.

Which brings me to the thralls.

Let's not pretend this isn't also a glorified waifu collection simulator.

You can tell yourself you're capturing thralls to improve your crafting efficiency, defend your fortress, or establish a thriving settlement. And sure, that's technically true. But sooner or later you're spending an unreasonable amount of time hunting down attractive NPCs, dressing them in increasingly impractical armor, and arranging them around your palace like some kind of deranged barbarian interior decorator.

And I love it. The gratuitous nudity, absurd violence, dismemberment, and unapologetically adult atmosphere are part of the charm. This is Conan the Barbarian, not a Disney theme park. It's supposed to be savage, bloody, ridiculous, and occasionally horny. The game embraces that identity, and I appreciate that it doesn't feel compelled to apologize for it.

Unfortunately, Funcom also knows exactly how much I enjoy decorating my fortress and dressing up my collection of barbarian murder-waifus, which brings us to the Bazaar. The microtransaction shop can be an obnoxious, overpriced cash grab. Some of the cosmetic sets are fantastic, but the pricing frequently borders on insulting. And yet, despite my principled objections to these business practices, I have personally contributed far too much money to perpetuating them. Apparently my outrage has a price, and that price is a particularly attractive set of Stygian furniture or another outfit for my digital harem. I am part of the problem. I accept this.

There are other frustrations, of course. The game can be buggy, the AI is inconsistent, some systems feel unfinished, and the developers occasionally introduce changes that leave me wondering whether anyone involved actually plays the game. But the underlying experience is so compelling that I keep coming back.

And that's ultimately what separates Conan Exiles from much of its competition.

Valheim has its exploration and atmosphere, but its endless resource grind and tedious bosses eventually wear out their welcome. Enshrouded has phenomenal building and more fluid combat, but it never quite captures Conan's sense of danger or its wonderfully savage identity. Plenty of survival games do one or two things better, but very few manage to bring exploration, combat, survival, construction, atmosphere, and settlement building together into such a satisfying package.

There's also something uniquely enjoyable about building a fortress in a hostile wilderness, filling it with warriors, craftsmen, dancers, and questionable architectural choices, and then heading out with your wife to explore some forgotten dungeon where you're both likely to die horribly.

Conan Exiles is janky, occasionally infuriating, shamelessly monetized, gloriously violent, and thoroughly ridiculous.

It's also still my benchmark for what a survival crafting game should aspire to be.

Now, if you'll excuse me, I have to go complain about predatory microtransactions while purchasing another decorative bathtub for my fortress full of mostly naked women.

I spent the night huddled next to the sheer cliffs by the beach. I was caught between a rock and a hard place. There was a brigand camp just a bit up the road, and the beach was infested with giant crocodiles which, I hoped, would be asleep.  The huge moon rose over the mountains lighting everything with its eerie light. On the horizon, magical flares erupted with a crackling sound that gave me a start. I clutched the razor-sharp falcata sword that I found on the body of a bandit who'd attacked me a few days ago. If only I knew how to make such wondrous swords! The best that I was able to achieve myself was a primitive stone cleaver. That's why I was here, on this hostile shore, away from my humble camp, looking for ironstone which, I had heard, could be used to smelt that most valuable of all metals - iron. Armour, swords, iron-tipped arrows… all of these would be mine if only I could survive this adventure. I didn't dare to start a campfire and I welcomed the first rays of the sun with gratitude, even though I knew I would curse it during the day as it scorched my already brown-tanned skin. A beast roared as the sun rose and an avalanche of stones rumbled down a slope in the distance. I braced myself, ate the remnants of my dried fish and set off deeper into this dangerous but beautiful desert land. 

To be honest, I bought this game because it was on sale, and I never expected it to bo so utterly, amazingly good. I'm quite critical of  modern games, which usually seem to be all about monetization. Here, I've played it for two days non-stop and I can see I'm only just beginning to comprehend how vast it is, even though I don't have any DLC. I've only visited a fraction of the map and I love the grind, which isn't too bad but you're not progressing too quickly either. As a result, you really get into the vibe of a lone exile, trying to survive on the edges of civilisation. 

A trek across the land, hiding from creatures that I know are too powerful to fight, gingerly skirting their territories, shows how fragile you still are at level 20, even though you might think you're tough because you've killed some minor creatures and fought off humans. Animals are territorial, they don't chase you forever like in some other games. They just want you to leave their territory but if you don't, they'll attack.  They fight also with each other (I don't think I've seen this in any other game), not because they're scripted to do so but because their territories might overlap.  

Character customisation is great, especially with a few basic mods from the Steam workshop. 

One more thing: the music.  To be honest, I normally switch music off in most games. Usually it's pretty generic, bombastic stuff that becomes boring rather quickly. This is different. The music is very varied, well suited to what's happening and adds to the suspense in combination with the amazing sounds of the jungle, roars of distant animals etc.  

All in all, so far - a great game, even if you're not a fan of the Conan universe.

### Conan Exiles: A Game That Left Its Most Dedicated Console Players Behind 



I have spent an enormous amount of time 4854 hours and money on **Conan Exiles**. Like many long-time players, I supported this game through DLCs, expansions, cosmetics, and countless hours of gameplay. That is why it is so disappointing to see the direction the game has taken for console players.

The biggest problem is not that Conan Exiles is an old game. Games age. The problem is that **the players who supported Conan Exiles for years feel like they have been left behind.**

Funcom has continued moving forward with enhanced versions and newer technology, while a large portion of the existing console community has been left dealing with an experience that increasingly feels outdated and neglected.

### Console Players Paid for the Game — Yet Feel Like Second-Class Players

Many console players have spent hundreds of dollars supporting Conan Exiles over the years.

We bought the expansions.

We bought the DLC.

We bought the cosmetic packs.

We invested thousands of hours into our characters, bases, clans, and servers.

And yet when improvements and enhanced technology arrive, those same players can be left wondering: **What exactly did all that support get us?**

The expectation isn't unreasonable. Players aren't asking Funcom to give us something for nothing. We are asking for the same level of attention and consideration given to other platforms.

### The Server Experience Has Become a Major Problem

One of the biggest issues is server performance.

Lag, rubber-banding, delayed actions, disconnects, and inconsistent server performance can make the game incredibly frustrating.

For a survival game where combat, building, farming, and PvP all depend on server responsiveness, this isn't a minor inconvenience.

**Server performance is the game.**

When you can spend hours building something, gathering resources, fighting enemies, and maintaining a character only to have the experience ruined by server problems, it becomes difficult to justify continuing to play.

### And Then There Is the Population Problem

Another major issue is the declining player population.

It becomes a vicious cycle:

Fewer players means fewer active servers.

Fewer active servers means fewer people to play with.

Fewer people playing means even more players leave.

Eventually, longtime players log in and find that the world they invested so much time into simply doesn't feel alive anymore.

That is particularly frustrating when the game itself still has tremendous potential.

Conan Exiles could still be an incredible long-term survival MMO-style experience. The foundation is there. The problem is that the community needs to feel like Funcom actually wants to keep those players.

### The Community That Supported Conan Exiles Should Matter

What bothers me most is the feeling that the people who helped keep this game alive are being forgotten.

Content creators, streamers, server owners, modders, clans, and everyday players spent years creating communities around Conan Exiles.

They promoted the game.

They brought their friends into the game.

They bought the DLC.

They maintained servers.

They created videos and streams.

They built enormous communities around it.

Those people weren't just customers. **They were part of what made Conan Exiles successful.**

When those players start saying they feel abandoned, Funcom should be listening.

### Curators, Streamers, and the Players Who Actually Supported the Game

There is also a growing disconnect between how the game is presented and what many longtime players actually experience.

You can watch streams, promotional content, curated gameplay, and videos showing Conan Exiles at its best.

But longtime console players know that the actual experience can be very different.

A game can look great in a curated video while the average player is dealing with lag, low-population servers, technical problems, and an aging console experience.

That doesn't mean streamers or creators are doing anything wrong. It means **Funcom needs to address the difference between the best-case presentation of Conan Exiles and the day-to-day experience of the players who have supported it for years.**

### This Isn't About Wanting Everything for Free

I want to make that clear.

This isn't a complaint from someone expecting endless free upgrades.

The complaint is about **value and respect for the existing customer base.**

If players have spent years buying DLC and supporting the game, they should not feel like their platform has been abandoned while the company moves on to newer technology.

At some point, you have to ask:

**Why should a player continue investing money into a game when they aren't confident that their platform and community will continue to receive meaningful support?**

### Conan Exiles Still Has Potential

The frustrating part is that I still like Conan Exiles.

That's why this criticism exists.

If I didn't care about the game, I wouldn't bother writing this.

Conan Exiles has one of the best foundations for a survival game: building, exploration, combat, thralls, clans, sieges, crafting, progression, and an enormous world.

But the game needs more than new cosmetics and additional monetized content.

It needs **investment in the player experience.**

It needs better server performance.

It needs a healthy population.

It needs meaningful support for console players.

And most importantly, it needs to show longtime customers that their years of support actually mean something.

### Final Verdict

**Conan Exiles is a great game that is increasingly difficult to recommend to longtime console players.**

The game itself deserves better.

The community deserves better.

And the players who have spent years and hundreds of dollars supporting Conan Exiles deserve better.

Funcom shouldn't look at longtime console players as an old customer base that can simply be left behind.

**We are the people who supported Conan Exiles when it needed us.**

Now it's time for Funcom to show that it still supports us.
